etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin polītus (“polished”), past participle of poliō (“I polish, smooth”); see polish.

quote.text: He marries, bows at court, and grows polite.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter IV, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I told him about everything I could think of; and what I couldn't think of he did. He asked about six questions during my yarn, but every question had a point to it. At the end he bowed and thanked me once more. As a thanker he was main-truck high; I never see anybody so polite.

quote.citation: 1704, I[saac] N[ewton], “(please specify |book=1 to 3)”, in Opticks: Or, A Treatise of the Reflexions, Refractions, Inflexions and Colours of Light. […], London:  […]  Sam[uel] Smith, and Benj[amin] Walford, printers to the Royal Society, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: rays of light  […] falling on  […] a polite surface

definitions.definition: (obsolete, transitive) To polish; to refine; to render polite.

quote.citation: 1691, John Ray, The Wisdom of God Manifested in the Works of the Creation. […], London:  […]  Samuel Smith, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: those exercises plied, which polite men's spirits
